claims.text: Single-crystal FeNiCrCoCu has been investigated as a nanoindentation system using molecular dynamics.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating is supported on a single-crystal Cu matrix.
The initial coating is a stable FCC solid solution with low dislocation density.
At 600 K, dislocation density decreases slightly while the lattice remains ordered, increasing elastic modulus and preserving wear resistance.
Above 900 K, deformation changes from dislocation-mediated plasticity to localized amorphization.
A temperature-driven reduction in stacking-fault stability causes the collapse of partial-dislocation dissociation.
Collapse of stacking-fault stability is followed by annihilation of the dislocation network and dislocation starvation.
Dislocation starvation is followed by formation of a disordered, amorphous-like shear band.
High configurational entropy and thermal energy above 900 K destabilize FCC stacking faults in FeNiCrCoCu.
At lower temperatures, plastic deformation proceeds through dislocation glide or multiplication rather than amorphization.
The amorphous layer behaves as a low-viscosity lubricant and initially lowers friction.
Loss of strain-hardening capacity in the amorphous zone causes catastrophic material removal and loss of wear resistance.
Ploughing by the indenter through the unstable softened zone causes the friction coefficient to spike.
Above 900 K, friction increases sharply while hardness and wear resistance decrease precipitously.
A decrease in HCP-classified atom count indicates loss of crystalline order.
A nonlinear reduction in total dislocation line length indicates dislocation annihilation rather than multiplication.
OVITO provides a DXA implementation that can be used for dislocation-line analysis.
Radial distribution function analysis can detect the onset of amorphization.
Artificially maintaining a high stacking-fault energy would prevent partial-dislocation collapse.
In polycrystalline material grain-boundary sliding may dominate, while lower strain rates may permit diffusion-assisted recovery.
